issues.legal_issue: Treating real-estate allottees as financial creditors does not violate constitutional equality, occupational freedom, or property protections.
material_facts: The legislative record identified frequent delays and failures in real-estate projects and found that advances from allottees substantially finance construction.
Allottees have a direct interest in the financial health of the developer because project completion or recovery of their advances depends on it.
The insolvency process is aimed at resolving the corporate debtor and is not a debt-recovery mechanism; an allottee who triggers it risks delay or loss rather than assured repayment.

Real-estate projects and promoter conduct are subject to regulatory disclosures, and developers may contest whether an allottee is entitled to payment or whether an insolvency application is being used fraudulently or maliciously.
issues.conclusion: The amendments classifying allottees as financial creditors are constitutionally valid and do not infringe Articles 14, 19(1)(g) read with 19(6), or 300-A.
issues.legal_principle: Economic legislation attracts a presumption of constitutionality and judicial deference; classification need not be perfect if it has an intelligible basis and a rational connection to the legislative purpose. The Court applied Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India (2019) 4 SCC 17; Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar (1959) SCR 279; State of Gujarat v. Shri Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974) 4 SCC 656; V.C. Shukla v. State (Delhi Administration), 1980 Supp SCC 249; Venkateshwara Theatre v. State of A.P. (1993) 3 SCC 677; and Mardia Chemicals Ltd. v. Union of India (2004) 4 SCC 311. It also applied the manifest-arbitrariness test discussed in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) 9 SCC 1.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_economic_ins: A litigant challenges an economic insolvency amendment that changes the treatment or rights of a class of creditors.
predicates.allottee_advances_finance_project: Purchasers pay money in advance that the developer uses to finance construction of their project.
predicates.allottee_has_stake_in_project_completion: Purchasers depend on the developer's financial health for completion of the project or recovery of their advances.
predicates.legislative_record_identifies_project_de: The legislative record identifies recurring delays or failures in the relevant sector.

issues.definition: When an economic insolvency amendment is challenged and purchasers' advances finance projects in which they have a direct stake, against a legislative record of recurring delays, the amendment is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: Insolvency remedies and real-estate regulatory remedies may operate concurrently, with the insolvency regime prevailing in the event of conflict.
material_facts: The real-estate regulatory legislation states that its remedies are in addition to, and not in derogation of, other laws.
The insolvency legislation contains an overriding clause, and the relevant amendment was enacted after the real-estate regulatory legislation.

The two regimes address different matters: one protects individual purchasers through project regulation and remedies, while the other provides a collective process focused on rehabilitation of the corporate debtor.
issues.conclusion: The two regimes are to be read harmoniously and provide concurrent remedies; if they conflict, the insolvency regime prevails.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the overriding provision in Section 238 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and Sections 88 and 89 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act. It relied on KSL & Industries Ltd. v. Arihant Threads Ltd. (2015) 1 SCC 166 and Bank of India v. Ketan Parekh (2008) 8 SCC 148 on resolving conflicts between statutes with overriding clauses, and on Swaraj Infrastructure Private Limited v. Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited (2019) 3 SCC 620 concerning parallel remedies.

predicates.overlapping_insolvency_and_real_estate_r: A purchaser can seek relief under both an insolvency process and a real-estate regulatory regime concerning the same project or default.
predicates.real_estate_law_preserves_other_remedies: The real-estate regulatory framework provides that its remedies supplement rather than displace remedies under other laws.
predicates.insolvency_regime_is_later: The applicable insolvency regime or amendment was enacted after the relevant real-estate regulatory regime.

issues.definition: When remedies under both regimes overlap, the real-estate regime preserves other remedies, and the insolvency regime is later, the remedies remain concurrent and the insolvency regime controls any conflict.

issues.legal_issue: Advances paid by allottees under real-estate project agreements qualify as financial debt, and the statutory explanation confirming that treatment is clarificatory.
material_facts: Allottees pay instalments to developers before their apartments or buildings are completed.
The payments are used to finance construction, while the allottee receives the completed property or an equivalent payment in return.
The allottee parts with the use of money for the construction period and ordinarily pays less than the price of a completed property.
The legislative committee considered the treatment of allottees uncertain and recommended expressly clarifying their status as financial creditors.
issues.conclusion: Allottees were included within the relevant financial-debt provision from the inception of the Code; the later explanation merely clarified that position.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(6), 3(11), and 3(12) define claim, debt, and default; Section 5(8), particularly clause (f), covers amounts raised through transactions having the commercial effect of a borrowing. The Court held that advance instalments finance a project and are paid for the time value of money, with the property constituting something equivalent to repayment. It relied on Innoventive Industries v. ICICI Bank (2018) 1 SCC 407; Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India (2019) 4 SCC 17; and Nikhil Mehta and Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. It distinguished Union of India v. Raman Iron Foundry (1974) 2 SCC 231 because the Code's definition of claim includes rights to payment arising from breach whether or not reduced to judgment. It also applied the principles on deeming provisions in East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council (1952) AC 109 and the interpretation of statutory explanations in S. Sundaram Pillai v. V.R. Pattabiraman (1985) 1 SCC 591.

rule.if: financial_creditor_status_dispute_under_insolvency_law and allottee_pays_before_project_completion and advances_fund_construction and payment_is_for_time_value_of_money

predicates.financial_creditor_status_dispute_under_: A proceeding disputes whether a purchaser under a real-estate project agreement is a financial creditor in an insolvency process.
predicates.allottee_pays_before_project_completion: A purchaser pays the developer before the contracted property is completed.
predicates.advances_fund_construction: The developer uses the purchaser's advance payments to finance construction of the project.
predicates.payment_is_for_time_value_of_money: The purchaser gives up use of money during the construction period in return for the future property or an equivalent payment.

issues.definition: When a financial-creditor-status dispute concerns a purchaser who pays before completion, finances construction, and parts with money for the construction period, that purchaser is a financial creditor.

issues.legal_issue: The mechanism for representing numerous financial creditors through an authorised representative is constitutionally valid despite differences among creditors in the class.
material_facts: Real-estate projects may have numerous allottee-creditors, and allottees may have different interests concerning possession, refunds, and compensation.
Allottees may fund a substantial part, or all, of a project and have a direct interest in its future.

The statutory mechanism provides for an authorised representative to attend creditor-committee meetings and vote for represented creditors; the later legislative amendment also provided for a class decision by majority voting share on specified matters.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the creditor-representation provisions was rejected; the representation mechanism is valid.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 21(6A) and 25A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, the relevant insolvency regulations on authorised representatives, and the subsequently enacted provision concerning class voting. It relied on Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India (2019) 4 SCC 17 for legislative latitude in economic matters and concluded that practical difficulties in implementation do not invalidate the mechanism.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_creditor_rep: A litigant challenges the legal mechanism for representing a creditor class in a collective insolvency proceeding.
predicates.creditor_class_is_numerous: The creditor class includes enough members to make individual participation in meetings impractical.
predicates.creditors_have_material_stake_in_debtor_: The creditors have advanced funds and are directly affected by the debtor's or project's future.
predicates.authorised_representative_can_convey_cla: A representative can participate in creditor meetings and communicate the voting decision of the creditors represented.

issues.definition: When a challenged representation mechanism concerns a numerous class with a material stake and allows a representative to convey the class vote, the mechanism is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory period for the adjudicating authority to decide whether default has occurred is directory rather than mandatory.
material_facts: The insolvency legislation specifies a period for the adjudicating authority to ascertain whether default has occurred.
The legislation provides no consequence for exceeding that period.
The adjudicating authorities faced a substantial volume of proceedings and insufficient members to determine them promptly.
issues.conclusion: The decision period is directory, not mandatory.
issues.legal_principle: A procedural time limit is directory where the legislation specifies no consequence for non-compliance and treating it as mandatory would obstruct justice. The Court applied Surendra Trading Company v. Juggilal Kamlapat Jute Mills Company Limited (2017) 16 SCC 143, and relied on State of Bihar v. Bihar Rajya Bhumi Vikas Bank Samiti (2018) 9 SCC 472 and its discussion of Kailash v. Nanhku (2005) 4 SCC 480.

predicates.proceeding_requires_adjudicating_authori: An insolvency proceeding requires an adjudicating authority to determine whether a default has occurred.
predicates.decision_period_is_procedural: The prescribed period regulates the timing of the adjudicating authority's decision rather than defining the substantive right or jurisdiction.
predicates.legislation_specifies_no_consequence_for: The governing legislation states no consequence for the adjudicating authority's failure to decide within the prescribed period.

issues.definition: When an insolvency proceeding requires a default determination within a procedural period and the legislation attaches no consequence to delay, the period is directory.

issues.legal_issue: Clear and unambiguous provisions that have been held constitutionally valid cannot be read down to impose additional limits not found in their text.
material_facts: The challengers proposed adding thresholds or preliminary inquiries before an allottee could trigger insolvency proceedings.
The Court had upheld the constitutional validity of the provisions and found their language clear and unambiguous.
The Court concluded that the adjudicating authority could consider legitimate defences within the existing statutory framework.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to read down the provisions in the manner proposed.
issues.legal_principle: Reading down is available in limited circumstances to preserve constitutionality or resolve ambiguity, but not to alter clear and unambiguous language or remake a statute. The Court relied on Cellular Operators Association of India v. TRAI (2016) 7 SCC 703, DTC v. Mazdoor Congress, 1991 Supp SCC 600, and the principles concerning reading down discussed in Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, In re, 1941 SCC OnLine FC 3.

predicates.request_to_read_down_insolvency_provisio: A litigant asks the court to add limits or conditions to an insolvency provision through interpretation.
predicates.provision_is_clear_and_unambiguous: The provision's language expresses a definite meaning without relevant ambiguity.
predicates.provision_has_been_upheld_as_constitutio: The court has determined that the challenged provision is constitutionally valid.

issues.definition: When a litigant seeks added limits to a clear provision that has been upheld as constitutional, reading down is unwarranted.
